Original Article
Theoretical and experimental study on the influence of fiber orientation on the tensile properties of unidirectional carbon fiber/epoxy composite

Author links open overlay panel,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aej.2022.12.058Get rights and content
Under a Creative Commons license
open access

Abstract

Probably-one of the most popular advantages of fiber-reinforced polymer composites is the capability to tailor their mechanical properties and, therefore, their behavior to an externally applied load. Regarding the layup manufacturing process, fiber orientation plays a fundamental role in the tensile resistance of carbon fiber-reinforced epoxy CFRE composites. Therefore, this work is aimed to realize a better understanding of the influence of fiber orientation on the tensile properties of CFRE composites. The study is conducted mathematically and experimentally on test samples with 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° fiber orientations. The maximum tensile stress values obtained from tensile tests are compared to the calculated ones through four basic failure models; maximum stress, maximum strain, Tsai–Hill, and Tsai–Wu. The results of the investigation indicate that the error between theoretical and measured values are highly affected by the fiber orientation of the composite. The experiments demonstrate that the resistance of CFRE composite to the tensile loading is mainly dependent on the fiber orientation. In particular, test specimens with 0° fiber orientation show maximum failure resistance (σ = 2857 MPa) compared to other orientations. Additionally, the orientation of fiber is found to have a substantial influence on the composites’ Young’s modulus. Maximum tensile strain at Yield (7.1 %) is obtained at 45° fiber orientation. The findings are anticipated to be guidelines for the design optimization of CFRE composite subjected to pure tension force.

1. Introduction

Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites are well known for their favorable properties such as low weight, high stiffness, high specific strength, low cost, corrosion resistance, and being eco-friendly [1], [2]. Also, one of their outstanding characteristics is the inherent anisotropy which gives the designer a facility to tailor the composites to realize the anticipated requirements. Due to these characteristics, laminated FRP composite materials are broadly applied in automotive, aerospace, sports, coating, pipelines, and electronics industries [3], [4]. Polymer resin and fiber reinforcement types, and fiber lay-up and fabrication methods are chosen and evaluated according to the desired engineering applications [5].
Carbon fiber-reinforced epoxy composites (CFRE) are gaining popularity as high-performance synthetic materials manufactured from the combination of two, or more, different phases of materials [6]. They are superior materials with high stiffness, strength properties workable up to 2000 °C (3632 °F), low density, and long fatigue life over many other conventional composites [7], [8]. Thanks to their excellent mechanical properties, they were broadly introduced in a variety of structural applications such as aerospace, automotive, and construction industries. The two main essential phases in developing CFRE composites are polymer matrix and fiber reinforcement [9]. The combination of these phases results in versatile mechanical properties that cannot be accomplished with a single material. Carbon fibers (CF) have 93 to 95 % carbon content and are produced at about 1300 °C (2372 °F). Epoxy resin, on the other hand, has been of substantial significance to engineering for many decades. Furthermore, composite materials made of fiber/epoxy combination have provided outstanding thermal, mechanical, and electrical properties [10].
Generally, the design of FRP structures needs knowledge of the stresses and strains in the composite individuals as well as in the bulk lamina. Experimental studies including tension, bending, torsion, and impact tests are frequently introduced to determine the mechanical properties of polymer composites [6], [11]. This data could be, also, theoretically obtained by the mechanical analysis of the lamina, or by modeling methods [12].
The global characteristics of FRP composite materials are affected by many factors [10]. The orientation of the fiber is considered a vital parameter that affects the mechanical response of composites [13]. Therefore, many previous and current researches are aimed to examine the influences of fiber orientation on the mechanical characteristics of FRP composites [14], [15], [16]. Banakar et al. [17] experimentally investigated the role of fiber orientation on the mechanical properties of CFRE. The composite laminates were fabricated from bi-woven weft-type carbon fiber and epoxy resin. The tensile resistance of the composites was explored at ± 30°, ±45o, and ± 90° orientation angles. The strength properties were superior in the case of 90° fiber orientation because the applied tensile load was distributed, in an equal manner, on all the fibers and transmitted along the axis of the fibers. However, Keshavamurthy et al. [18] observed that the maximum Yield strength, stiffness, and load-carrying capacity realized at the 0° fiber orientation in ply laminated glass fiber reinforced epoxy GFRE composites. Bassey et al. [19] introduced an experimental and analytical study of the consequence of fiber orientation and fiber content on the tensile strength of GFRE composites using the Taguchi experimental technique. They suggested that 45° fiber orientation and 50 % fiber content resulted in the optimum tensile strength of the tested composite. Patl et al. [9] explored the impact of fiber orientation on the tensile strength of thin CFRE composites fabricated using bi-directional woven reinforcements. Through the Bi-directional carbon fiber three fiber orientations were selected for testing: [0°/90°], [30°/60°], and [45°/−45o]. The results obtained from tensile tests established that the highest tensile strength was obtained at 0°/90° fiber orientation in which flat failure and fiber delamination were detected. In the weft direction, fibers remained undamaged, while in the warp direction, fiber pullout and fiber breakage were found. It is also inferred that the specimens with 30° and 45° fiber orientation had lower tensile strength than those with a 0° fiber orientation. They postulated that the tensile force acting on fiber laminate divided into warp and weft directions.
Finding comprehensive literature that consider the effect of orientation in the case of unidirectional fiber laminated composites is still difficult. In fact, to the best of our knowledge, only a few studies considered such an aspect. Rahmani et al. [20] documented the influence of fiber orientation on the mechanical properties of unidirectional CFRE laminated composites. The tensile properties in terms of modulus, strength, and elongation at break were examined following ASTM D-638 (2014) [21], [22] standard method using a universal testing machine (STM-150). The effect of fiber orientation was determined at angles of 0°, 35°, 45°, and 90°. The composites with 0°, 35°, 0o, and 0°, –35°, 0°, +35°, and 0° orientations showed the highest tensile strengths and moduli among the tested composites. The scanning electron microscopy (SEM) examination of tested specimens suggested that the failure mechanism was attributed to fiber fracture due to tensile force. The micrographs showed that there is no evidence of fiber pull-out, matrix cracking, interface debonding, or interlaminar delamination. As also recently pointed out by Parmiggiani et al. [23], the influence of the fiber orientation on the tensile properties of unidirectional CF/Nylon composites was significantly justified if the fibers were aligned with the direction of the applied tensile load (i.e., at 0° orientation). Additionally, the variation of both elastic modulus and tensile strength was not linear with the angle between fibers' direction and the tensile load. A quick deterioration in mechanical properties was notably detected when increasing the fiber angle to + 45°. The related failure modes and stress–strain curve of the 0° orientation specimen suggested high strength and stiffness, along with little deformation capability. Consequently, sudden brittle rupture of the specimens was expected as soon as breakage of the CF occurred.
Concerning the above-mentioned studies, the tensile characteristics of unidirectional CF-reinforced polymer composites are highly affected by fiber orientation. However, there is no unique agreement about the most critical orientation. Thus, there is a massive need for more research to enrich comprehensive knowledge in such cases. The present work aims to identify the influence of fiber orientation on the mechanical properties of CFRE when subjected to tensile load. The theoretical data determined from the strength failure theories are compared with those obtained experimentally from simple tension tests.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Preparation of the test specimen

The materials used for the fabrication of composite test samples were unidirectional carbon fiber UNIC200 yarns supplied by SELCOM SRL, Diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A epoxy resin (EPOLAM 2017®), and 3-minomethyl-3,5,5 trimethylclohexylamine hardener (EPOLAM 2018®). Both the epoxy resin and the hardener were supplied by Axson (the chemical formula is shown in Fig. 1). Table 1, Table 2 present the properties of carbon fiber and epoxy matrix respectively.

According to the manufacturer’s recommendation, the ratio of 10:3 was selected for mixing epoxy resin and hardener. The hand-lay-up method was used to produce the composite laminates of rectangular shape. Using a thick glass mold, the unidirectional laminates were produced by placing the carbon fiber plies layer by layer, according to the desired orientation, with an epoxy matrix in between the layers. Hand tools were applied to acquire a uniform distribution of resin as well as to remove entrapped air. To ensure proper curing of the composite, the mold was kept closed under pressure for 1 day at 25 °C. In the current study, 4 layers of fiber plies were applied to fabricate composite plates that have a total thickness of about 0.8 mm. Through the fabrication process, five different composite plates were prepared with different orientation angles of the reinforcing carbon fiber to the longitudinal axis: 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°. Fig. 2 shows (a) the angle (θ) of layer orientation with longitudinal direction and (b) the glass mold and the preparation of carbon fiber ply. The test specimens were cut from the prepared composite plates following ASTM D3039 (2014) [24]. The obtained samples, as shown in Fig. 2(a), have a rectangular shape of dimensions 240 mm × 18 mm × 0.8 mm and were nomenclated as 0, 30, 45, 60, and 90 test specimens (the dimensions of the coupons were determined with a vernier caliper). Carbon fiber/epoxy end-tabs with a thickness of 4 mm were glued to the ends of all samples to minimize stress concentration near the grips of the tensile testing machine. The final gauge length of the samples was kept constant at 240 mm.

2.2. Experimental method

Following ASTM D-638, all tensile tests were performed using a Servo-hydraulic Universal Testing Machine UTM 600 kN (Mod. TT-HW2-600) with a electronic control unit with resolution of ± 500,000 steps, and measuring accuracy of +/-0.5 %. An extensometer was used to measure the longitudinal strain, as shown in Fig. 3. The composite specimen was placed and aligned between the grippers. During the test, a specimen was subjected to controlled tension at a fixed strain rate of 2 mm/min until fracture. The load at which the fracture of the specimen occurred has been reported as a breakage load [13], [25]. For safety reasons, the testing machine was programmed to stop at the breaking point (i.e., at the sharp drop in the applied tension load). The specimen elongation was determined from the cross-head movement of the test machine where the obtained stress–strain curve was used to determine the tensile properties of the composites. The values reported here are the arithmetic average of two replicate tests. To recognize failure patterns in the composite specimen, optical micrographs were taken using SEM, and images were captured using an HD digital camera.

2.3. Mathematical calculations

2.3.1. Global stresses

The composite materials often contain more than one lamina which has a small thickness (≈ 0.125 mm) [1], [2]. Unlike isotropic materials, the mechanical properties of the lamina vary from point to point depending on whether the point is in the matrix, the fiber, or the interface between them. To overcome this complication, the macro-mechanical analysis of a lamina is based on the mean properties assuming the lamina is homogeneous.
In the present study, these average properties are calculated based on the individual mechanical properties of the fiber and the matrix given above in Table 1, Table 2 and tabulated in Table 3. The equations used to determine the global mechanical properties can be found elsewhere [26], [27].

2.3.2. Local stresses

As shown in the Figure, the local axes in the 1–2 coordination contain a longitudinal direction 1 which is parallel to the fibers, and a transverse direction 2 which is perpendicular to the fibers. On the other hand, the axes in the x-y coordinate system are called global axes. The angle between the two axes is denoted as (θ).

Failure of a lamina has been determined by various theories which are generally based on the normal and shear strengths of a unidirectional lamina [30]. In the current study, we will determine the maximum global and local stresses in the composite sample following four common failure theories:

2.3.3. Maximum stress failure theory [T1]:

According to this theory, the failure occurs in a lamina if the normal (or shear) stresses in the local axes are equal to or greater than the corresponding ultimate strengths of the unidirectional lamina. which can be represented mathematically as [31]:(5)-σ1Cult<σ1<σ1Tult,or(6)-σ2Cult<σ2<-σ2Tult,or(7)-τ12ult<σ6<τ12ult
where.
σ1Tult ultimate longitudinal tensile strength in direction 1,
σ1Cult ultimate longitudinal compressive strength in direction 1,
σ2Tult ultimate transverse tensile strength in direction 2,
σ2Cult ultimate transverse compressive strength in direction 2, and.
τ12ult ultimate in-plane shear strength in plane 1–2.

2.3.4. Maximum strain failure theory [T2]:

According to this theory, the failure occurs in a lamina if the normal (or shear) strain in the local axes is equal to or greater than the corresponding ultimate strain of the unidirectional lamina. which can be given by [31]:(8)-ε1Cult<ε1<ε1Tult,or(9)-ε2Cult<ε2<ε2Tult,or(10)-Y12ult<Y6<Y12ult
where
ε1Tult ultimate longitudinal tensile strain in direction 1,
ε1Cult ultimate longitudinal compressive strain in direction 1,
ε2Tult ultimate transverse tensile strain in direction 2,
ε2Cult ultimate transverse compressive strain in direction 2, and.
Y12ult ultimate in-plane shear strain in plane 1–2.

2.3.5. Tsai-Hill failure theory [T3]:

The theory advocates that failure will take place in a material when the distortion energy becomes greater than the failure distortion energy [32]. Based on this hypothesis, the lamina will fail if:σ1(σ1T)ult2-σ1σ2(σ1T)ult2+σ2(σ2T)ult2+τ12(τ12)ult2<1(11)
However, the Tsai-Hill equation does not distinguish between tensile and compressive strengths, which may result in underestimation of the maximum loads that can be applied when compared to other failure theories.

2.3.6. Tsai-Wu failure theory [T4]:

Compared to the Tsai-Hill theory, the Tsai-Wu theory is more general because it can distinguish between tensile and compressive strengths of a lamina [32]. According to this theory, a lamina is considered to be failed if:(12)H1σ1+H2σ2+H6τ12+H11σ12+H22σ22+H66τ122+2H12σ1σ2<1

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Study of failure modes

Scanning electron microscopy images of fractured tensile test specimens of composites were investigated and analyzed in order to understand the failure in the fiber–matrix interaction zone. It was advocated that the failure mode of composites was attributed to the fiber orientation and there were, typically, three distinct patterns of failure detected under longitudinal tensile loading, as illustrated in Fig. 5. Fig. 6 (a) shows the failure pattern during tensile testing of specimens with θ = 0° orientation. The figure suggested that the failure in the composite was due to fracture and pull-out of carbon fibers, and matrix fracture. The existence of some small holes and traces of matrix resin adhering to the fiber advocated strong bonding in the fiber/matrix interface, and consequently, the fibers provided an efficient stress transfer from the matrix. This mode of failure is matched with the results obtained from the tensile test, where the maximum tensile stress and maximum strain were found in 0° orientation. In reality, under tensile load, failure in CFRE takes the form of isolated interfacial microcracks increasing in number with loading and finally coalescing into a catastrophic macrocrack [35]. Similar findings by Seshaiah et al. [36], Hossein Rahmani et al. [20], and others [3], [4], [5] suggested that due to this strong interphase, composites undergo individual fiber breakage appreciably.
Conversely, for the composite samples with θ = 90° orientation, failure was attributed to transverse matrix cracking, as shown in Fig. 6 (b). Delamination of fibers and flat failure of the matrix were frequently observed rather than fiber breakage. The fracture surfaces of specimens seemed to be flat, smooth, and free from any polymer adhering to the fiber. The interfacial adhesion between the fiber and the polymer matrix is very poor which suggests the lower stress values in this orientation. For orientation angles between 0° and 90°, the fracture edge is preferred to grew along the direction of carbon fibers, as illustrated in Fig. 5 (c). Optical images of broken specimens after tensile testing are shown in Fig. 7. In all specimens, the cracks of the polymer matrix have the same angle as the carbon fibers.

The experimental results, shown in Fig. 8, advocated that the 0° orientation of the carbon fiber is the favorable direction to resist tension forces in unidirectional CFRE laminated composites. The maximum tensile stress obtained in 0° orientation was about 10 folds to those found in other orientations, as presented in Table 6. The most accepted explanation for this observation is that the carbon fibers are aligned with the direction of the tension force and bear the load alone rather than the epoxy matrix. The load is equally distributed on all the carbon fibers and transmitted along the fiber axis [8]. The polymer matrix, in this case, seems to have no significant impact on the specimen strength. Notably, the maximum strain in 0° orientation was (4 %) which is very close to the arithmetic mean of the individual fiber and matrix, as presented in Table 1, Table 2. This hypothesis becomes more evident by observing typical failure modes, as shown in Fig. 5 (a), and 6 (a), which makes it clear that properties such as high strength and stiffness, along with little deformation capability, led to sudden and brittle fracture of the specimens [23].
Another observation was realized while increasing the angle of fiber orientation to 90° (i.e., perpendicular to the direction of applied load), where a dramatic loss in mechanical resistance was detected. The composite recorded the minimum value of tensile strength (σx = 58 MPa) which is about 0.15 % lower than that of epoxy resin, given in Table 2. Although it might be logic to expect that the samples, in the 90° orientation test, should behave as a pure polymer because the fibers are not subjected to tensile load. In fact, the transverse fibers have a converse effect on the tensile strength of the samples. Typical failure modes, shown in Fig. 5 (b) and 6 (b), support this point of view where the fracture of the samples ran transversally to the principal specimen/load direction. Debonding in the polymer matrix is clearly observed as a consequence of the progressive distancing of carbon fibers initially adjacent [11]. Specimens with 30°, 45o, and 60° fiber orientations showed similar modes of fracture nonetheless cracks propagated diagonally following the fiber direction, as shown in Fig. 5(c) and Fig. 7. At these orientations, the composite becomes softer and easier to deform and so the elongation becomes larger. The fracture of the samples occurred once the failure of the epoxy matrix took place [37].
Probably-one of the interesting observations in the stress–strain curve is the remarkable tensile strain (7.1 %) of the 45° orientation specimens which is about 0.18 % greater than epoxy resin and about 380 % greater than carbon fiber. A similar observation was previously declared by Kumar et al. [25] and Seshaiah et al. [36] that during tensile tests the fiber/epoxy composites with 45° fiber orientation showed more elongation compared to those of other orientations.
The reason for such an observation could be twofold. From a deformation standpoint, the presence of the CF unavoidably supports the deformation of the composite material which may increase the overall elongation at break values. It is postulated that in the 0° orientation (loading along CF direction) the stiffness of the composites reaches its highest value where the lowest stiffness is obtained when this angle is around 45° which exhibited the maximum elongation at the break value.
On the other hand, regarding the mechanical performance of CFRP composites, it should be taken into consideration that the carbon fibers embedded in the epoxy matrix are involved in the mechanical resistance of the test samples. Thus, the maximum tensile strain will be affected by the efficiency of the matrix-to-fiber interfacial conditions, fiber orientation, fiber volume fraction, and other factors. At 45° fiber orientation, stress transfer between the fiber and the matrix is highly reduced due to the less matrix content in the composite which is a good reason for the reduction in tensile strength.

3.3. Effect of fiber orientation on Young’s modulus of unidirectional CFRE

In order to get a comprehensive understanding of the tensile behavior of composites, we will discuss the obtained stress–strain curves in terms of Young’s modulus (E) as described in Section 2.3.7. The plane of isotropy at every point in the CFRE composite is considered aa an independet isotropic material. In the present study, according to Table 4, the first element in the 6 × 6 compliance matrix in Equation (17) is Young’s modulus of loading direction (x-direction). For a unidirectional lamina, the elastic constants are:
E1 longitudinal Young’s modulus (in direction 1).
E2 transverse Young’s modulus (in direction 2).
ν12 major Poisson’s ratio.
G12 in-plane shear modulus (in 1–2 plane).
Considering that the 2–3 plane in the plane of isotropy at a given point inside the CFRE composite, the requirements for transverse isotropy are: E2=E3=Ep,ν12=ν13=νtp,ν21=ν31=νpt,andG21=G31=Gt, where t and p stand for “transverse” and “in-plane”. Using Equation (27), the flexibility matrix (C) can be written as:(27)C=0.008-0.0020.0001000-0.0020.17-0.002000-0.002-0.0020.170000000.220000000.220000000.35
The stiffness matrix D is:(28)D=C-1=125.351.47-0.0560001.495.90.070001.490.095.90000004.550000004.550000002.86
Substituting the above results in Equation (26), Young’s modulus (Ex) as a function of fiber orientation (θ) is:(29)Ex=125.35cos4θ+5.9sin4θ+4.55sin2θcos2θ
Equation (29) is used to draw a theoretical relationship between Young’s modulus and the fiber orientation angle of the CFRE composite, as shown in Fig. 9. The values of Young’s modulus obtained experimentally, Table 7, were also used to plot another curve (experimental). According to the figure, it is postulated that the theoretical elastic modulus (E) decreases monotonically from its maximum value (E1 = 125.35 GPa) at θ = 0° to its minimum value (E2 = 5.9 GPa) at θ = 45°.
There is an acceptable agreement between the elastic modulus that is estimated theoretically and the data obtained experimentally. The values of elastic modulus are approximately the same in analytical and experimental cases, except for θ = 45° which was underestimated. This may be explained in Fig. 8, where specimens having 45° fiber orientation exhibited a maximum elongation (minimum Young’s modulus) before fracture versus those of other orientations because of the deformation ability of the CF composite in this direction. Another possible explanation for this drawback is due to the effect of shear modulus which is primarily governed by matrix behavior and has a substantial influence on the modulus of elasticity, especially at a 45° angle of orientation [33].
It is worth pointing out that the experimental results, shown in Fig. 9, indicated a U-shaped dependency of the composite Young’s modulus on the orientation angles of the fiber. The minimum value of Young’s modulus (i.e., lowest stiffness) is obtained at 45° orientation. The same trend was also advocated by Wang, H.W. et al. [33] as they introduced an analytical and experimental confirmation for the U-shaped tendency. An insignificant difference between theoretical and experimental results was reported. Analytically, Young’s modulus should reach its lowest value at 60° orientation, but the experimental results indicated that the minimum value is found around 45°. This discrepancy is attributed to: (1) the difference between actual and theoretical composite properties, and (2) the simplifications made for solving the analytical model.
Regarding maximum stresses (σx), the error between predicted and measured values presented in Table 5, Table 7 was used to plot Fig. 10. According to the figure, the overall agreement between the theoretical and experimental results can be recognized in 0° and 90° orientations. Except for the data obtained from the Tsai-Wu failure theory, the general error in predicting maximum stress values at 0° and 90° orientations was less than 1 %. Nonetheless, at the 30°, 45°, and 60° orientations, the values of error ranged from 2.6 % to 31.2 % while no clear trend could be deduced.
A possible conclusion that could be drawn from these findings is that the accuracy of data obtained from failure theories is highly affected by the CFRP configuration. Furthermore, this discrepancy could rely on several criteria covering the failure modes of the composite; fiber failure, matrix failure, and delamination. Such failure patterns can be further classified as (a) non-interactive and (b) interactive failure criteria [38].
  • (a)
    Non-interactive failure criteria do not consider the interaction between stresses/strains acting on the lamina. This includes maximum stress and maximum strain failure theories which showed good agreement with experimental results only in principal directions (in 0° and 90° fiber orientations) where the failure of the composite was due to fiber fracture (at 0° orientation), or matrix fracture (at 90° orientation). On the contrary, maximum stress and maximum strain theories failed to predict accurate stress/strain values at other fiber orientations (30°, 45°, and 60°) where the failure of composite is governed by the fiber/matrix interaction.
  • (b)
    Interactive failure criteria where the interaction between stress/strains acting on each lamina are considered. These are Tsai-Hill, and Tsai-Wu failure theories where failure mechanisms associated with both matrix and fiber failures are considered. The values resulting from applying these theories showed errors (up to 17 %) compared with experimental results, as shown in Fig. 10.

4. Conclusions

This work was conducted to explore the effect of the orientation of carbon fibers reinforced epoxy CFRE on the tensile response of composite materials. The optimized performance of the proposed CRFE composite was realized when the CFs were aligned in the same direction as the acting force. In particular, tensile tests were performed at composite samples with five selected orientations 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90°. Along with the experimental work, a theoretical study was performed to predict maximum tensile stress of the composites using four well-known failure theories: maximum stress, maximum strain, Tsai-Hill, and Tsai-Wu. Based on the experimental and theoretical findings we can highlight the following:
  • 1.
    From the tensile testing of CFRE composites, the 0° orientation exhibited a maximum failure resistance value (σ = 2857 MPa) compare to other orientations while the minimum value (σ = 58 MPa) was obtained at 90° orientation. Consequently, when varying the fiber orientation to 45°, the composite showed a maximum tensile strain at Yield (7.1 %) compared to all specimens.
  • 2.
    Failure of composite specimens (0° orientation) was due to sudden and brittle fracture of the samples, while at 90° orientation the fracture of the specimens ran transversally (perpendicular to the applied load). Other fiber orientations showed similar fracture mode to what was observed at 90° orientation, however, cracks propagated diagonally inside the polymer matrix following the fiber direction.
  • 3.
    SEM of 0° orientation fractured coupons provided some evidence of fiber pull-out and fiber fracture, while at 90° orientation transverse matrix fracture and fiber delamination were detected.
  • 4.
    The theoretical calculations could be a possible solution to predict the tensile properties for 0° and 90° orientations for CFRE composites with an acceptable error (less than1%). However, the accuracy of the predicted data was highly affected by both the configuration of the CFRE composite and the applied model. In this context, values of the error ranged from 2.6 % to 31.2 % when applying the aforementioned failure theories with the 30°, 45°, and 60° orientations.
  • 5.
    Analysis of the potential impact of fiber orientation on Young’s modulus suggested a U-shaped relationship curve, with a minimum value of Young’s modulus at 45° orientation.
Future work
Following the promising data obtained from this work, the authors will extend their research to explore the potential effect of hole notch on the mechanical behavior of CFRE composite at different fiber orientations.
